doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23

title: Potatoes in horns, Limburger cheese and boy bandsmen
summary: Laine denies the potato story, describes pranks like limburger in a horn and how he kept his young players in line on out-of-town trips.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Well, sometime Nick LaRocca told about that you used to have some of the men put potatoes in the horns. Do you remember that? Well...

The fellas that couldn't play? I'll tell you what happened. We played... We played for Martin Borman in the old St. Charles Hotel frame building. You understand? Yeah. And it was his campaign, running for mayor. My first daughter mayor. Was it Alfred put Limburger cheese in...
All the skin, the team got the Limburger cheese, you know how nice that smells. He put that down in his...

He filled his heart up with Limburger cheese. Man, it smelled something horrible. Every time he'd blow in it, that... You know that odor. It'd knock you... Yeah, they used to put stuff in them. Them kids used to play. Every one of them. They were up to all kinds of stuff.
LaRocca talked like if you'd hire somebody sometime that couldn't play at all, you'd put a potato in the horn so they couldn't make any noise to hurt anything.
He said that you did that, I think. I did. Yeah, on some of the men that they couldn't play. Do you remember that? Ever putting potatoes in their horns so they couldn't play?
No, no, no. I remember playing jokes on men that played music.

That really played music. They said, fellas take it off, they don't take their socks off and shove it down. Yeah. That's all of that sort of stuff. Well, they used to play to miss them kids, you know. We were all youngsters then, you know. They were terrible. I had a handful to handle them. They were over home with her all the time, a whole bunch of them. I had a garret, a big open garret, you know. Had beds up in there. And when I'd take a job out of the city, I wouldn't trust them buggers. I'd make them come and stay by me. See? I'd get them up early in the morning, maybe five o'clock, maybe half past four train, leaving from the LNN or whatever road it was, early. Now, I'm just as sure as the almighty God in heaven, Joe Stevens is dead in his grave today. It's a mighty good thing that there were two trains going to Biloxi that morning. Stevens over slept, and simply missed the first train, and I just had time enough to go down to his house. He lived on Tulu, Tulu's, or St. Louis Street, near the Cedar. And the railroad, of course, was right up here, canal in the river. A few blocks. And get him out, and get him on time to get that train to make that job in Biloxi. As almighty God told. Overstepped himself. But when I come there, they were up. They were up. When I came there, the minute that train pulled out and I didn't see him there, you know, I said, well, I found out that there was another train followed pretty shortly. I said, let me see if I can make it. With God sending, I made it. I got Rag Baby Stevens out on time.
